lessons.title: Role of builders in detergents
lessons.body:
Builders are the workhorses of a detergent formula. They soften water by tying up calcium and magnesium ions that would otherwise stop soap and surfactants from cleaning. In many African cities, water hardness can be 200-500 mg/L as CaCO3. Without builders, you waste surfactant and get poor cleaning. Builders also provide alkalinity to break down acidic soils like grease and oils, and they help keep dirt suspended so it rinses away.

Common builders include sodium carbonate (washing soda), sodium silicate, zeolites, and citrates. In a typical powder detergent for hand washing, you might use 20-30% sodium carbonate and 5-10% sodium silicate. For machine washing, zeolites or polycarboxylates are better because they don't leave deposits. Builders also affect pH. Most laundry detergents work best at pH 9-10.5. You can test pH with cheap pH strips from a pharmacy or agricultural shop.

In Africa, builders are often the cheapest way to boost cleaning power. For example, in Nigeria, a common formulation uses 25% sodium carbonate, 10% sodium silicate, and 5% zeolite. This mix costs less than adding more surfactant. However, too much builder can damage fabrics or cause skin irritation. Always wear gloves and a dust mask when handling powders.

To test builder effectiveness, mix a small batch with and without builder, wash soiled cloth swatches (e.g., with palm oil or clay), and compare. You can also measure water hardness with a simple titration kit. If you use borehole water, builders are essential. For soft water (rainwater), you can reduce builder amount by half. Remember, builders are not a replacement for surfactants; they work together. A good rule: if your detergent doesn't lather well in local water, increase builder or add a chelating agent like citrate.

lessons.title: Inorganic builders: zeolites, carbonates, silicates
lessons.body:
Inorganic builders are minerals that soften water and provide alkalinity. The three most common are zeolites, sodium carbonate, and sodium silicate. Zeolites are hydrated aluminosilicates, like Zeolite A (Na12Al12Si12O48Â·27H2O). They exchange sodium ions for calcium and magnesium, softening water without creating scum. In Africa, zeolites are imported but affordable. Use 15-25% in powder detergents. They work best at 60Â°C but also function at lower temps. Zeolites are insoluble, so they need a dispersant like polycarboxylate to prevent deposits on clothes.

Sodium carbonate (washing soda, Na2CO3) is the cheapest builder. It precipitates calcium as CaCO3, but that precipitate can redeposit on fabric. Use 20-40% in hand-wash powders. It also raises pH to 10-11, which helps remove grease. In East Africa, soda ash is mined in Kenya (Lake Magadi) and is very cheap. Sodium silicate (Na2SiO3) is a corrosion inhibitor and builder. It forms a protective layer on metal parts of washing machines and helps keep dirt suspended. Use 5-10% in powders. It also adds alkalinity and can be bought as a liquid (water glass) or powder.

When mixing, add silicates last because they can gel. Wear a dust maskâsilicate dust is harmful. For a simple hand-wash powder: 30% sodium carbonate, 10% sodium silicate, 15% zeolite, 15% surfactant (e.g., LABSA), 20% sodium sulfate, and 10% other additives. Test by washing oily cloths in hard water. If white spots remain, reduce carbonate and increase zeolite. If cloth feels stiff, reduce silicate. In rural areas, you can make a builder mix of 70% soda ash and 30% silicate for boosting soap. Store in airtight bagsâcarbonates absorb moisture.

lessons.title: Organic builders: citrates, polycarboxylates
lessons.body:
Organic builders are biodegradable and work well in hard water without leaving precipitates. The two main types are citrates and polycarboxylates. Sodium citrate (Na3C6H5O7) is made from citric acid, which can be fermented from cassava or maize starch. It chelates calcium and magnesium, softening water. Use 5-15% in liquid or powder detergents. Citrate is especially good for eco-friendly products. In Africa, you can buy sodium citrate or make it by reacting citric acid with soda ash. It works best at pH 8-9, so combine with a little carbonate.

Polycarboxylates are synthetic polymers like polyacrylic acid (PAA) or acrylic-maleic copolymers. They are excellent at dispersing zeolites and preventing soil redeposition. Use 2-5% in powders with zeolites. They are not fully biodegradable but are used at low levels. In liquid detergents, use 1-3% sodium polyacrylate. These builders are more expensive than carbonates, so use them where needed: for machine washing, for anti-redeposition, or for hard water above 300 mg/L.

A practical African formulation for a liquid detergent: 10% LABSA, 5% sodium citrate, 2% polycarboxylate, 3% sodium carbonate, 2% sodium silicate, and water to 100%. Adjust pH to 9 with citric acid. For a powder: 20% zeolite, 5% citrate, 3% polycarboxylate, 25% carbonate, 10% silicate. Test by washing in hard water and checking for greyness. If clothes grey, increase polycarboxylate. If water doesn't soften, increase citrate. Citrates are also food-safe, so they are good for cleaning food surfaces. Store polycarboxylates in dry placeâthey can absorb moisture.

lessons.title: Bleaching agents and activators
lessons.body:
Bleaching agents remove stains and whiten fabrics by oxidation. The most common is sodium percarbonate (2Na2CO3Â·3H2O2), a solid form of hydrogen peroxide. It releases oxygen in water, especially above 60Â°C. In Africa, many washes are done at lower temperatures, so you need activators. Tetraacetylethylenediamine (TAED) is the main activator. It reacts with percarbonate to form peracetic acid, which works at 40Â°C. Use 1-3% TAED with 10-20% percarbonate in powder detergents.

Another bleach is sodium hypochlorite (liquid bleach), but it damages fabrics and is not compatible with enzymes or fragrances. Use it only for white cotton and disinfecting. For color-safe bleaching, use percarbonate with TAED. You can buy percarbonate from chemical suppliers; it's often sold as 'oxygen bleach'. In Kenya or Nigeria, check with soap-making suppliers. TAED is imported but affordable.

Formulation tip: mix percarbonate and TAED dry, and keep away from moisture. Add 0.5% of a chelating agent like EDTA to stabilize. For a bleach booster: 70% sodium percarbonate, 20% TAED, 5% sodium carbonate, 5% citrate. Use 10-20 g per wash. Test by soaking stained cloth (tea, tomato, grass) in warm water with 5 g/L booster for 30 minutes. Rinse and compare. If stains remain, increase percarbonate or temperature. For low-temp (30Â°C), use more TAED. Note: percarbonate loses activity over timeâstore in sealed bags away from heat. Never mix with chlorine bleach. For hand washing, wear gloves; percarbonate can irritate skin.

lessons.title: Enzymes: proteases, amylases, lipases
lessons.body:
Enzymes are proteins that break down specific stains. Proteases break down proteins (blood, egg, grass), amylases break down starches (rice, pasta, chocolate), and lipases break down fats (oil, butter, gravy). They work at low temperatures (30-50Â°C) and are used at 0.5-2% in detergents. In Africa, enzymes are imported as liquid or granulated powders. Store them cool and dry; heat above 60Â°C destroys them.

For a powder detergent, use granulated enzymes coated for stability. Add them last in the mixing process, after the powder has cooled. For liquid detergents, use liquid enzymes and avoid high pH (above 10) and high surfactant levels that can denature them. A typical liquid enzyme mix: 0.5% protease, 0.5% amylase, 0.2% lipase. You can buy these from suppliers like Novozymes or local distributors. They are expensive, so use only if your market values stain removal.

Practical test: soak stained cloths in a solution of 2 g/L detergent with and without enzymes at 40Â°C for 30 minutes. Rinse and compare. You'll see better removal of protein and starch stains with enzymes. For oily stains, lipase helps but needs more time. In hard water, enzymes work less well, so use a builder. Also, never mix enzymes with chlorine bleachâit destroys them. For a budget enzyme booster: 50% protease, 30% amylase, 20% lipase, mix and use 1-2 g per wash. Keep in a cool, dark place. In West Africa, some entrepreneurs make enzyme-rich detergents using local papain from pawpaw, but it's less stable. Stick to commercial enzymes for consistency.

lessons.title: Optical brighteners, fragrances, and dyes
lessons.body:
Optical brighteners (OBAs) are dyes that absorb UV light and re-emit blue light, making fabrics look whiter and brighter. They don't clean but improve appearance. Common OBAs are stilbene derivatives, like Tinopal. Use 0.1-0.5% in powder or liquid detergents. In Africa, OBAs are imported and can be expensive. For a cheap alternative, some use small amounts of blue dye (e.g., ultramarine blue) to mask yellowing, but OBAs are more effective. Add OBAs to the detergent base after surfactants, and mix well. For liquids, dissolve OBA in a small amount of water first.

Fragrances make detergent pleasant and signal cleanliness. Use 0.5-2% of a fragrance oil. In Africa, you can buy local essential oils like lemongrass, eucalyptus, or citrus, but they may be less stable. Synthetic fragrances are cheaper and stronger. Add fragrance last, at low temperature, to prevent evaporation. For powders, spray fragrance onto the powder while mixing. For liquids, add with gentle stirring. Test by smelling washed cloth after 24 hours; if too weak, increase.

Dyes are used to color the detergent itself, not the clothes. Use 0.001-0.01% of a dye like Acid Blue 9 or food coloring. Too much dye can stain fabrics. For a green detergent, use a few drops of green dye per liter. Always add dye diluted in water. In a powder, mix dye with a small amount of sodium sulfate to avoid clumps. A simple brightener/fragrance/dye premix: 10% OBA, 20% fragrance, 1% dye, 69% sodium sulfate. Use 1-2% of this premix in your detergent. Store in dark containers. Test on white cloth: wash with your detergent and compare to a control. If cloth looks blue, reduce OBA. If it smells too strong, reduce fragrance. Remember, these additives don't affect cleaning but drive customer satisfaction.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Builders and Additives in Detergent Manufacturing

This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in the Builders and Additives module and turns them into a working tool for African detergent producers. Builders and additives typically account for 25â45% of raw material cost in a powdered or liquid laundry detergent, and they determine whether your product performs in hard water, meets regulatory limits, and carries a margin you can defend. Use this page alongside your batch sheets, supplier quotations, and lab test records.

1. What Builders Do and Why They Matter Commercially

Builders perform four jobs: they soften water by binding calcium and magnesium, they supply alkalinity to saponify fats, they help disperse and suspend soil so it does not redeposit, and they buffer pH during the wash. In African markets, water hardness is the single most common cause of customer complaints about "the powder does not foam" or "clothes come out grey." A well-built formulation handles hardness up to 300â500 mg/L as CaCOâ, which covers much of the continent's groundwater. If you sell in a hard-water city, builder level is a competitive weapon, not a cost line to cut.

2. Inorganic Builders: Zeolites, Carbonates, Silicates

Zeolite A (sodium aluminosilicate) is the workhorse of phosphate-free powders. It exchanges sodium for calcium inside its cage structure. It is insoluble, so it needs a co-builder (usually polycarboxylate) to prevent it depositing on fabric. Typical use: 15â30% in powder.

Sodium carbonate (soda ash) is cheap, locally available in Kenya, Nigeria, Egypt, and South Africa, and provides alkalinity. It precipitates calcium as CaCOâ, which is acceptable in powders with good anti-redeposition agents but can cause incrustation on fabric if overused. Typical use: 10â25%.

Sodium silicate provides alkalinity, protects washing machine metal parts from corrosion, and acts as a binder in spray-dried powder. It also helps control powder density and flow. Typical use: 2â8%.

3. Organic Builders: Citrates and Polycarboxylates

Sodium citrate is biodegradable, safe, and effective in liquid detergents where zeolite would settle out. It sequesters calcium but has lower capacity per gram than zeolite, so it is used at 5â15% in liquids. It is a strong marketing point for "eco" or "green" lines.

Polycarboxylates (e.g., sodium polyacrylate, acrylic-maleic copolymers) are co-builders. They boost zeolite performance, disperse calcium carbonate crystals, and prevent soil redeposition. Typical use: 1â5%. They are poorly biodegradable, so keep levels low and disclose in your MSDS.

Table 1: Typical builder levels and cost indicators for a powdered laundry detergent (30 g/L wash dose)
BuilderFunctionTypical % in powderIndicative cost bandAfrica sourcing note
Zeolite AIon exchange (Ca/Mg)15â30%MediumImported; check local blending capacity
Sodium carbonateAlkalinity, precipitation10â25%LowLocally produced in KE, NG, EG, ZA
Sodium silicateAlkalinity, corrosion, binder2â8%LowâmediumOften local; verify solids content
Sodium citrateSequestration, biodegradable5â15% (liquid)MediumâhighImported; good for premium lines
PolycarboxylateCo-builder, anti-redeposition1â5%MediumâhighImported; low dose keeps cost down

Source: Ranges compiled from Smulders, E. (2002), Laundry Detergents, Wiley-VCH; and Bajpai, D. & Tyagi, V.K. (2007), Journal of Oleo Science, 56(7), 327â340. Cost bands are indicative only and must be replaced with current supplier quotations.

4. Bleaching Agents and Activators

Sodium percarbonate (2NaâCOâÂ·3HâOâ) releases hydrogen peroxide in warm water and is the standard oxygen bleach for colored and white fabrics. It is stable in powder if kept dry and below 40Â°C in storage. TAED (tetraacetylethylenediamine) is the activator: it reacts with peroxide to form peracetic acid, which bleaches effectively at 40Â°C instead of 60Â°C. This matters commercially because most African households wash at ambient temperature; without an activator, your bleach is largely wasted. Typical levels: percarbonate 10â20%, TAED 1â4%.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Bleach and Enzyme Handling

Never mix sodium percarbonate or any peroxide bleach with chlorine-releasing compounds or with concentrated acids: toxic chlorine gas can be released. Store percarbonate away from heat, moisture, and organic matter (it is an oxidizer and can accelerate fire). Enzyme powders are respiratory sensitizers: wear a P2/N95 mask and eye protection when weighing proteases, amylases, or lipases, and never handle them in the same open area as bleach. In many African production sites, dust control and PPE are the weakest link â fix ventilation before increasing batch size. Follow the supplier SDS and your national OSHA/health and safety authority requirements.

5. Enzymes: Proteases, Amylases, Lipases

Enzymes let you cut surfactant and builder levels while improving stain removal. Proteases break down protein stains (blood, egg, grass, milk). Amylases attack starch stains (rice, cassava, porridge, potato). Lipases hydrolyze fats and oils (cooking oil, body sebum). Typical total enzyme dose in a powder is 0.3â1.5% of active enzyme granulate; in liquids, 0.2â1.0%. Enzymes are inactivated by high pH, high temperature, and free chlorine. In Africa, the biggest enzyme risk is heat: unventilated warehouses in Lagos, Mombasa, or Khartoum can exceed 40Â°C and destroy activity. Store in a cool, dry place and rotate stock on a first-in-first-out basis.

6. Optical Brighteners, Fragrances, and Dyes

Optical brighteners (fluorescent whitening agents, FWAs) absorb UV light and re-emit blue light, making white fabric look brighter. Typical dose: 0.05â0.3%. They work on cotton and cellulosics; on polyester they are less effective. Fragrances are the strongest driver of repeat purchase in African retail â a customer often buys the smell. Typical dose: 0.1â0.5% for powder, 0.2â0.8% for liquid. Choose fragrance concentrates that survive spray drying or, better, dose post-drying. Dyes at 0.001â0.01% give visual identity; keep them lightfast and check compatibility with bleach.

Table 2: Additive dosing guide and common failure modes
AdditiveTypical doseWhy it fails in the fieldFix
Optical brightener0.05â0.3%Yellowing on repeated use; poor on syntheticsMatch FWA type to fabric; test after 10 washes
Fragrance0.1â0.8%Fades in storage; lost in spray dryingUse encapsulated or post-dosed fragrance
Dye0.001â0.01%Stains fabric; fades in lightUse lightfast dye; run stability test
Protease0.3â1.5%Activity lost in hot storageCool store, FIFO, check activity on receipt
TAED1â4%No bleach benefit at low wash tempConfirm activator:peroxide molar ratio
Sodium percarbonate10â20%Decomposes with moistureUse moisture barrier packaging; desiccant

Source: Doses compiled from Smulders, E. (2002), Laundry Detergents, Wiley-VCH; and from supplier technical data sheets for enzyme granulates and percarbonate (Novozymes, Evonik, Solvay). Always confirm with your own lab trials.

7. Quick Reference Checklist

  • Test your water first. Measure hardness (mg/L as CaCOâ) in your target cities before fixing builder levels; hard water needs more zeolite or citrate.
  • Balance builders with co-builders. Zeolite without polycarboxylate deposits on fabric â never skip the co-builder.
  • Match bleach to wash temperature. Below 50Â°C, use TAED or another activator, or the percarbonate is mostly wasted.
  • Protect enzymes from heat and moisture. Store below 30Â°C, use FIFO, and verify activity on each delivery.
  • Dose fragrance post-drying. Spray-dried fragrance is largely lost; post-dose for a stronger, cheaper scent claim.
  • Run a 10-wash fabric test. Check whiteness, greying, and brightener buildup on cotton and polyester before launch.
  • Keep SDS and labels current. Polycarboxylates, enzymes, and percarbonate all require correct hazard communication.
  • Calculate cost per wash, not cost per tonne. A cheaper builder that needs a higher dose can cost more per wash.

8. Further Reading

  • World Bank / IFC â Environmental, Health, and Safety Guidelines for Soap and Detergent Manufacturing (free PDF, covers effluent, dust, and PPE).
  • UNEP â Global Chemicals Outlook and SAICM resources on detergent ingredients and phosphates.
  • US EPA â Safer Choice Ingredient List (free database of detergent ingredients and health/environment profiles).
  • African Development Bank â Industrialization and SME manufacturing reports for market and financing context.
  • ISO â ISO 4316:1977 Surface active agents â Determination of pH of aqueous solutions (paywalled abstract, free scope summary).

Business note: in most African markets, the winning formulation is not the most advanced one â it is the one that performs in local hard water, survives local storage heat, carries a fragrance customers remember, and still leaves a margin after transport and retail markup. Use this reference to set your builder and additive levels, then validate with a 10-wash test and a cost-per-wash calculation before you scale the batch.

quiz.q: What is the main role of builders in a detergent?
options: B) To soften water by binding calcium and magnesium
quiz.explanation: Builders soften water by chelating or precipitating hardness ions, allowing surfactants to work effectively.

quiz.q: Which builder is a hydrated aluminosilicate?
quiz.explanation: Zeolites are crystalline aluminosilicates that exchange sodium ions for calcium and magnesium.

quiz.q: What is a common percentage of sodium carbonate in a hand-wash powder?
quiz.explanation: Sodium carbonate is a cheap builder used at 20-40% in many hand-wash formulations.

quiz.q: Which builder is known for inhibiting corrosion in washing machines?
quiz.explanation: Sodium silicate forms a protective layer on metal parts, reducing corrosion.

quiz.q: Which organic builder is biodegradable and can be made from citric acid?
quiz.explanation: Sodium citrate is a biodegradable chelating agent derived from citric acid.

quiz.q: What is the typical use level of polycarboxylates in a powder detergent with zeolites?
quiz.explanation: Polycarboxylates are used at 2-5% to disperse zeolites and prevent soil redeposition.

quiz.q: Which bleaching agent releases hydrogen peroxide in water?
quiz.explanation: Sodium percarbonate is a solid form of hydrogen peroxide that releases oxygen for bleaching.

quiz.q: What is the role of TAED in a bleaching system?
options: A) It activates percarbonate to work at lower temperatures
quiz.explanation: TAED reacts with percarbonate to form peracetic acid, which is effective at 40Â°C.

quiz.q: Which enzyme breaks down starch stains?
quiz.explanation: Amylases hydrolyze starch into sugars, removing starch-based stains.

quiz.q: At what temperature range do enzymes typically work best?
quiz.explanation: Most detergent enzymes are active between 30Â°C and 50Â°C, with higher temperatures denaturing them.

quiz.q: Which of these should never be mixed with enzymes?
quiz.explanation: Chlorine bleach denatures enzymes, destroying their activity.

quiz.q: What is the function of optical brighteners?
options: B) To make fabrics look whiter by emitting blue light
quiz.explanation: Optical brighteners absorb UV light and re-emit blue light, masking yellowing and enhancing whiteness.

quiz.q: At what percentage are fragrances typically added to a detergent?
quiz.explanation: Fragrances are usually used at 0.5-2% to provide a pleasant scent without being overpowering.

quiz.q: Why should dyes be added in very small amounts?
quiz.explanation: Excess dye can transfer to fabrics during washing, causing unwanted coloration.

quiz.q: Which builder is best for eco-friendly formulations?
quiz.explanation: Sodium citrate is biodegradable and derived from renewable resources, making it eco-friendly.

quiz.q: What is a common symptom of too much builder in a detergent?
quiz.explanation: Excess builder can cause poor lather, skin irritation, and fabric damage due to high alkalinity or deposits.

quiz.q: Which test can help determine if your builder is working?
options: B) Washing soiled swatches in hard water
quiz.explanation: Washing soiled swatches in hard water and comparing results shows builder effectiveness.

quiz.q: What is the recommended pH range for most laundry detergents?
quiz.explanation: Most laundry detergents work best at pH 9-10.5 for optimal soil removal.

quiz.q: Which of these is an inorganic builder?
quiz.explanation: Sodium carbonate is an inorganic builder, while citrate and polycarboxylate are organic.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of zeolites over sodium carbonate?
options: B) They don't precipitate calcium as scum
C) They work at higher temperatures
quiz.explanation: Zeolites exchange ions without forming insoluble precipitates, reducing redeposition.

quiz.q: Which enzyme would be most effective against grass stains?
quiz.explanation: Grass stains contain proteins, which proteases break down.

quiz.q: How should enzymes be stored?
options: B) In a cool, dry place
quiz.explanation: Enzymes are sensitive to heat and moisture, so cool, dry storage preserves activity.

quiz.q: What is a common activator for oxygen bleach?
quiz.explanation: TAED is the most common activator that reacts with percarbonate to form peracetic acid.

quiz.q: Which additive is used to prevent soil from redepositing on fabrics?
quiz.explanation: Polycarboxylates disperse soil particles and keep them suspended in the wash water.

quiz.q: What is a cheap alternative to optical brighteners for masking yellowing?
quiz.explanation: A small amount of blue dye can counteract yellow tones, though less effectively than OBAs.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a builder?
quiz.explanation: Sodium chloride (table salt) is not a builder; it is used as a filler or for viscosity adjustment.

quiz.q: What is the typical percentage of sodium percarbonate in a bleach booster?
quiz.explanation: A bleach booster often contains 50-70% sodium percarbonate as the active bleaching agent.

quiz.q: Why should fragrance be added last in detergent production?
options: B) To avoid reaction with enzymes
quiz.explanation: Fragrances are volatile and can evaporate if added during hot mixing processes.

quiz.q: Which builder is mined in Kenya and is very cheap?
quiz.explanation: Sodium carbonate (soda ash) is mined at Lake Magadi in Kenya.

quiz.q: What is the main function of a lipase enzyme in detergent?
quiz.explanation: Lipases hydrolyze triglycerides, helping remove oily and fatty stains.
